title: Families Without Children Are Actually Freeloading Off Families With Children
dek: Liang Jianzhang's core argument: each child's future pension and innovation benefits are shared by society as a whole, but the cost of childbearing falls solely on parents—this is the fundamental logic behind his position that governments should provide real financial subsidies for childbirth, not merely moral exhortation.
why: A rare deep conversation spanning entrepreneurial history, cross-border strategy, remote-work experiments, and population-policy logic all at once—the back half on population and AI philosophy carries the highest information density.
who: Entrepreneurs, HR decision-makers, and policy researchers interested in corporate globalization strategy, remote-work effectiveness, or the logic of birth-rate policy.
skip: 0:35–24:25 covers childhood and Fudan youth-class experiences, leaning toward personal memoir—jump straight to 34:52 onward for the entrepreneurship section.

points.body: Liang Jianzhang sees himself as a beneficiary of accelerated learning: as a ninth-grader he focused on computer competitions, then self-studied high school mathematics, physics, and chemistry, and entered Fudan's youth class at fifteen, bypassing high school entirely. He therefore argues that gifted students should compress middle school, high school, and even college into accelerated paths—subjects like physics need only two passes, not three; the efficiency problem isn't the curriculum but the gaokao system locking everyone into the same pace.

points.h: Ctrip's four founders meshed in less than six months
points.body: Liang Jianzhang, Ji Qi, Shen Nanpeng, and Fan Min didn't have clearly defined roles initially and experienced friction, but the meshing period lasted only three to five months—soon Ji Qi handled external relations, Shen Nanpeng became CFO and handled fundraising, Liang Jianzhang focused on internal management and IT, and Fan Min brought hospitality-industry management experience. He attributes Ctrip's early success to two things: Six Sigma–style standardized processes that refined call-center scripts, and process and data management that achieved ticket distribution across all channels—airports, train stations, and aircraft.

points.h: 3+2 hybrid didn't hurt productivity because only Ctrip does it
points.body: After the pandemic, Ctrip ran a 3+2 hybrid-office experiment for engineers and other specialist roles and found no decline in code output or overall performance—employee satisfaction and loyalty rose noticeably. But Liang Jianzhang admits this partly depended on Ctrip being the only large Chinese company doing it—employees who compared themselves horizontally felt happier, and this may not generalize. Silicon Valley founders later privately told Luo Yonghao that while they publicly support hybrid work, they privately believe efficiency does fall; some admitted to playing basketball on remote days, only to encounter coworkers doing the same on the court.

points.h: Mobile Internet's lag forced a company-wide pivot
points.body: Around 2012, Ctrip lagged visibly in mobile development, lost market share, and faced price wars. Liang Jianzhang ended his academic career and returned as CEO. He created an independent mobile division, pulled in the best engineers, personally drove app development, and mandated that all product discussions use phone screenshots rather than desktop screenshots. In six months to a year, Ctrip's app went from lagging to industry-leading, and the organization shifted from centralized to divisional to accelerate iteration.

points.h: Ctrip went global eight years ago, not multi-category
points.body: Liang Jianzhang believed travel shouldn't stay confined to mainland China but should expand one category globally—a completely different path from Alibaba, Tencent, and Meituan's continuous category expansion domestically. Eight years ago, Ctrip acquired the Trip.com domain, first targeting Hong Kong and Taiwan, then Asia. Today it ranks first in Singapore and Malaysia, approaches first in South Korea, and leads in Japan flights. But he admits travel's supply chain is deeply local, and Ctrip still hasn't fully overtaken Booking's Agoda across Asia.

points.h: Demographic and economic experts' knowledge mismatch
points.body: When Liang Jianzhang studied innovation, he found Japan's shift from innovation boom to decline tracked closely with population decline. Looking at China's data, he discovered a puzzle: demographers hold the real data but think fewer people is good; economists readily accept population-shortage logic but lack accurate data. At the time, the public and policymakers still thought the one-child policy posed no problem.

points.h: Families without children freeload off families with children
points.body: Liang Jianzhang argues childbearing creates externalities: one child's future pension and innovation benefits the entire society, but childbearing's cost falls entirely on the family—so families who don't or rarely have children are freeloading off large families. He admits the claim easily provokes backlash (the "birth-encouragement bureau director" joke stems from this), but he insists it's the fundamental logic for government to provide real cash subsidies, not simply moral appeals to young people.

points.h: Innovation shouldn't go to AI—it lacks mortality
points.body: Liang Jianzhang says ChatGPT's biggest philosophical impact is this: in theory, neural connections can replicate nearly all human abilities. But he firmly believes technology innovation shouldn't be dominated by AI—AI's creativity inevitably brings uncontrollable hallucinations, whereas human ethical judgment springs from "having birth and death, instinctively wanting descendants to continue"—something AI can only simulate, never truly possess. When managing risk, he favors multiple small AIs that check each other, with human-verifiable intermediate steps, not a single black-box large model.

quotes.text: Does AI need population? Now that AI's here, do we still need innovation? Why have children at all? That's a philosophical question.

For example, if team members are constantly working together in person, some responsibilities may technically belong to A, but B and C naturally get involved too—because through daily close working proximity, people form certain emotional connections.

Frankly, our attitude—the attitude in Silicon Valley—is that if a company wants to go back to five days in the office, we absolutely won't do it; we'll just switch to a company with hybrid mode. But in all honesty, they also admit that efficiency does decline.
It's more of a gray rhino than a black swan—something you can already see coming from far away. Of course, you must act now; otherwise, you'll inevitably face problems twenty years from now.
Childbearing does have externalities—having children benefits the entire country. It doesn't just contribute to your own family's happiness; it genuinely benefits the entire society and nation.

Innovation and having children are both elevated forms of happiness-seeking. If you create new life, new technology, a new company, a new product, new art—that's a higher order of happiness than entertainment like gaming or even travel. Why hand that happiness over to a machine?
